'''Ezra Theodore Newman''' (October 17, 1929 – March 24, 2021)<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://obituaries.post-gazette.com/obituary/ezra-ted-newman-1081869139|title = Remembering the life of Ezra Ted Newman (1929–2021) |work=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]}}</ref> was an American physicist, known for his many contributions to [[general relativity]] theory. He was professor emeritus at the [[University of Pittsburgh]]. Newman was awarded the 2011 [[Einstein Prize (APS)|Einstein Prize]] from the [[American Physical Society]].

==Education==
Newman was born in the [[Bronx]], New York City to David and Fannie (Slutsky) Newman.<ref name=Debus>[[Allen G. Debus]] (1968) ''Who's Who in Science'', page 1250, [[A. N. Marquis]]</ref> He showed an early interest in science, pondering magnets, match flames, and science books.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Basken |first=Paul |title=A Humble Heavyweight in Physics Finally Gets His Due |date=February 13, 2011 
|url=https://www.chronicle.com/article/a-humble-heavyweight-in-physics-finally-gets-his-due/ |work=[[The Chronicle of Higher Education]] |access-date=February 16, 2022}}</ref>

He was admitted to the [[Bronx High School of Science]], where he excelled at physics.  Ted's father hoped that he would follow him into dentistry, but instead Ted enrolled at [[New York University]] to further his study of physics, graduating with a B.A. in 1951. For graduate education he went to [[Syracuse University]], obtaining an M.A. in 1955 and a Ph.D. the following year.<ref name="Physics Matters">{{cite magazine |title=Ezra (Ted) Newman |magazine=Physics Matters |date=September 2011 |publisher=[[Syracuse University]] |page=1 |volume=6 |url=https://answers.syr.edu/download/attachments/118785607/6%20Volume.pdf |access-date=16 February 2022}}</ref>

==Career in physics==
Newman joined the [[University of Pittsburgh]] faculty in 1956, becoming [[professor]] of physics in 1966. He was a visiting professor at Syracuse University in 1960/61 and at [[King's College London]], in 1964/65. In 1957 he served as consultant at [[Wright-Patterson Air Force Base]].<ref name=Debus/>

In 1962, together with [[Roger Penrose]], he introduced the powerful [[Newman–Penrose formalism]] for working with [[spinor]]ial quantities in general relativity. The following year he and coworkers extended [[Abraham H. Taub]]'s solution to the [[Einstein field equation]] obtaining the [[Taub–NUT space]].<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Newman, E. T. |author2=Tamburino, L. A. |author3  =Unti, T. |name-list-style= amp | title=Empty-space generalization of the Schwarzschild metric | journal=J. Math. Phys. | year=1963 | volume=4 | page=915 | doi=10.1063/1.1704018|bibcode = 1963JMP.....4..915N | issue=7 }}</ref> He also generalized the [[Kerr metric]] developed by [[Roy Kerr]] to include a charged body, resulting in the [[Kerr–Newman metric]].

In 1973 he advocated the use of [[complex number]]s in relativity, and consideration of [[complex spacetime]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Newman|first=E. T.|title=Maxwell's equations and complex Minkowski space|journal=[[Journal of Mathematical Physics]]|year=1973|volume=14|issue=1|publisher=The American Institute of Physics|doi=10.1063/1.1666160|bibcode = 1973JMP....14..102N|pages=102–103}}</ref>

Some of his most interesting recent work has involved the problem of reconstructing the gravitational field within some region from observations of how optical images are [[gravitational lens|lensed]] as light rays pass through the region.

In 2002 an email he forwarded to [[John C. Baez]] helped to touch off the [[Bogdanov Affair]].

Newman was selected as a Fellow of the American Physical Society in 1972.<ref>{{cite web |title=APS Fellow Archive |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=N |publisher=American Physical Society |access-date=2018-03-28}}</ref> In 2011, he was awarded the [[Einstein Prize (APS)]] "for outstanding contributions to [[Theory of relativity|theoretical relativity]], including the [[Newman–Penrose formalism]], [[Kerr–Newman solution]], Heaven, and [[foliation|null foliation]] theory, for his intellectual passion, generosity and honesty, which have inspired and represented a model for generations of relativists".<ref name="Physics Matters"/><ref>{{cite web | title=2011 Einstein Prize Recipient | url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Newman&first_nm=Ezra&year=2011 | access-date=November 21, 2010 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=GRG Editor's Choice: Classical mechanics via GR and Maxwell's theory: a bit of magic |journal=[[General Relativity and Gravitation]] |date=19 August 2018 |volume=50 |url=https://www.springer.com/gp/livingreviews/relativity/news/grg-editors-choice-classical-mechanics-via-gr-and-maxwell-theory/15990900 |access-date=16 February 2022 |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |language=en}}</ref>

==Family==
Newman married Sally Faskow on April 20, 1958,<ref name=Debus/> with whom he had two children, [[David Newman (physicist)|David E. Newman]], a professor of physics at the [[University of Alaska Fairbanks]], and Dara Newman.
